Where $\left(x\right)$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x.$ If $f$ is continuous on $R$, then $\left(a + b\right)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
We have,

$f\left(x\right) = \left( \begin{matrix}\sin x−{e}^{x} & \mathrm{if}x \le 0 \\ a + \left( - x\right) & \mathrm{if}0 < x < 1 \\ 2x−b & \mathrm{if}x \ge 1\end{matrix} \right)$

If $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = a$ then $\underset{x \to {a}^{ - }}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = f\left(a\right) = \underset{x \to {a}^{ + }}{\lim }f\left(x\right)$.

Continuous at $x = 0 f\left({0}^{ + }\right) = f\left({0}^{ - }\right) \implies a - 1 = 0 - {e}^{0} \implies a = 0$

Continuous at $x = 1 f\left({1}^{ + }\right) = f\left({1}^{ - }\right) \implies 2\left(1\right) - b = a + \left( - 1\right) \implies b = 2 - a + 1 \implies b = 3 ∴a + b = 3$

$f\left(x\right) = \left( \begin{matrix}{x}^{2}\sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right);x \ne 0 \\ 0;x = 0\end{matrix} \right) \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }\left({x}^{2}\sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\right) \implies \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }{x}^{2} \times \left(\mathrm{number}\mathrm{between} - 1\mathrm{to}1\right) \implies \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = 0 = f\left(0\right)$

Now,

$\mathrm{RHD} = {f}^{'}\left({0}^{ + }\right) = \underset{h \to 0}{\lim }\left(\frac{f\left(0 + h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{h}\right) \implies \mathrm{RHD} = {f}^{'}\left({0}^{ + }\right) = \underset{h \to 0}{\lim }\left(\frac{{h}^{2}\sin \left(\frac{1}{h}\right) - 0}{h}\right) \implies \mathrm{RHD} = {f}^{'}\left({0}^{ + }\right) = \underset{h \to 0}{\lim }\left(h\sin \left(\frac{1}{h}\right)\right) = 0$

And,

$\mathrm{LHD} = {f}^{'}\left({0}^{ - }\right) = \underset{h \to 0}{\lim }\left(\frac{f\left(0 - h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{ - h}\right) \implies \mathrm{LHD} = {f}^{'}\left({0}^{ - }\right) = \underset{h \to 0}{\lim }\left(\frac{ - {h}^{2}\sin \left(\frac{1}{h}\right) - 0}{ - h}\right) = 0$

Since, $\mathrm{LHD} = \mathrm{RHD} = \mathrm{finite}$

So, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable at $x = 0$.

Now,

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left( \begin{matrix}2x\sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) - \cos \left(\frac{1}{x}\right);x \ne 0 \\ 0;x = 0\end{matrix} \right)$

$\underset{x \to 0}{\lim }{f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }\left(2x\sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) - \cos \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\right) \implies \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }{f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }\left(2x\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{3!}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}} + \frac{1}{5!}\frac{1}{{x}^{5}} - ....\right) - \left(1 - \frac{1}{2!}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} + \frac{1}{4!}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}} - ....\right)\right) \implies \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }{f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \underset{x \to 0}{\lim }\left(\left(1 - \frac{2}{3!}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} + \frac{2}{5!}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}} - ....\right) - \left( - \frac{1}{2!}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} + \frac{1}{4!}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}} - ....\right)\right)$
